claims.text: Controlled aging can induce in situ nanoscale precipitates in a high-entropy alloy.
The aging-induced precipitates will be uniformly dispersed throughout the alloy matrix.
The aging-induced nanoscale precipitates will remain stable during elevated-temperature exposure.
Nanoscale precipitates hinder dislocation motion in the high-entropy alloy.
Nanoscale precipitates impede grain-boundary sliding in the high-entropy alloy.
Obstruction of dislocation motion by the precipitates enhances elevated-temperature yield strength.
Impediment of grain-boundary sliding by the precipitates enhances creep resistance during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The aging treatment will improve elevated-temperature yield strength by approximately 10–20% relative to a solutionized baseline.
The aging treatment will improve creep resistance by approximately 10–20% relative to a solutionized baseline.
The proposed improvement is expected generally above 600°C.
High-entropy alloys are relevant to extreme-environment and high-temperature applications.
Elevated-temperature nuclear-reactor service is an intended application boundary for the proposed intervention.
Elevated-temperature aerospace service is an intended application boundary for the proposed intervention.
The baseline is an otherwise identical solutionized or homogenized alloy without engineered nanoscale precipitates.
The applicability of the proposed improvement at other temperatures or loading conditions remains undetermined.
The exact improvement magnitude and long-term thermal stability of the precipitates remain uncertain.
The intervention can be tested by comparing aged and as-solutionized specimens using elevated-temperature tensile and creep tests together with TEM or SEM characterization.
Failure to obtain a greater-than-10% statistically significant mechanical improvement, or failure to observe nanoscale precipitates, is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
